fields.title: Integrations: someone else's system means someone else's decisions
fields.keyTakeaway: Integration is not "connecting an API," but an agreement on contract, failures, and ownership. Key questions: what happens when the other side is unavailable, and who fixes it when it breaks at night.
fields.checkQuestion: An integration with the cash register returned an item with an empty barcode. Who will notice, and what will the seller see?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key node question: **how will the product integration happen?**
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you don't answer the question.** Integration is treated as a technical detail and handed entirely to engineering. A month later, stock levels diverge across three stores, and no one can tell whose data is correct.
fields.blocks/2/title: What a PM must clarify before starting
fields.blocks/2/subtitle: Five questions, none of them technical
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **Who owns the data** — whose single source of truth wins in case of divergence. This is a business decision, not an engineering one.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **What happens during downtime** — queue and retry, explicit failure with a message, or silent loss. The third occurs more often than it seems.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **How often and with what delay** — once a minute or once a day; the user must understand how fresh the displayed data is.
fields.blocks/2/items/3: **What to do on divergence** — who resolves it, where it is visible, whether there is a manual override.
fields.blocks/2/items/4: **Who is responsible on failure** — your support or theirs; it's better to have an agreement before the first incident.
fields.blocks/3/text:
Agreed: cash register owns prices, Polka owns stock counts.

Cash register is offline: Polka displays the last known price with a label "data as of 14:20." The seller sees that the price is stale, which is better than an empty field.

Stock divergence: once a day a list is generated, and the shift supervisor inspects it at the end of the day. Nothing is automatically overwritten — the cost of an error is higher than saved time.

A two-week pilot in one store: during this time, found that the cash register was sending weighted items as units. Across forty stores, this would have cost a week of debugging.
fields.blocks/3/title: Polka and the Ritm cash register
fields.blocks/4/text: If data simply fails to deliver during downtime without signaling anyone, divergence accumulates for weeks and is discovered during inventory. Always ask what happens to an undelivered message.
fields.blocks/4/title: "Silent loss" — the most expensive failure mode
fields.blocks/5/text: An agreement with another team is not a guarantee. Versions change, fields disappear. Therefore, integration must have monitoring on your side: can you see if data stopped coming in, and how quickly will you know.
